catalog_quote: The rules for assigning stress are complex, and there is a lot of variation, resulting from several competing factors that determine stress. There is a general penultimate stress target, but, as in other Arnhem Land languages (Baker 2008a), stress is also quantity-sensitive ... The vowels /a/ and /ɛ/ tend to be longer than the other vowels ..., so they attract the stress and possibly disturb the general pattern of penultimate stress assignment. Closed syllables are also heavy and likewise attract stress. ... The following account is preliminary only and restricted to stress in isolated word forms. ... • The penultimate syllable of words is the primary stress target (Stokes 1981; Leeding 1989) ... • Stress may be shifted away from penultimate to antepenultimate position if the former contains a vowel other than /a/ or /ɛ/, while the latter does contain /a/ or /ɛ/ ... • Heavy syllables attract stress, where syllable weight is determined by the number of morae. Long vowels, diphthongs and closed syllables are bimoraic and are stress attractors. ... When the two principles of penultimate stress assignment and heavy syllables attracting stress compete, this may result in varying stress ... • An epenthetic vowel (rule P-1) never receives stress ... In summary, as in other Arnhem Land languages, stress in Enindhilyakwa is quantity-sensitive. There is a general penultimate stress target, but this can be disturbed by heavy syllables.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress targets the penultimate syllable; the system is weight/quality-sensitive: syllables with the inherently longer vowels /a, ɛ/ and closed syllables are heavy and can pull primary stress to the antepenult when the penult has only /i, ə/ (often with free variation between penult and antepenult); epenthetic vowels are never stressed; final stress does not occur except (per Leeding 1989) on the suffixes -aki/-tha. Leeding 1989 (p.140) and Stokes 1981 (p.157) independently give penultimate primary stress with a further stress on the first syllable (alternating/di-syllabic feet).
new_statements.secondary_stress: van Egmond: pronominal prefixes on verbs generally receive secondary stress; transcriptions show secondary stress on initial syllables (e.g. [ˌmakaˈʈuwa]). Leeding 1989 p.140: stress on first and penultimate syllables; in even-syllabled words on alternate syllables (first syllable of each disyllabic foot); in longer odd-syllabled words initial + penult with a trisyllabic first foot.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress when penult has /i, ə/ and antepenult has /a, ɛ/ or is closed (variable); variable stress with certain verbal TAM suffixes before -ma; epenthetic vowels never stressed even in penult; Leeding: intensifier -aki and terminaliser -tha stressed on final syllable; some trisyllabic suffixes prefer their own penult. van Egmond calls her account preliminary and notes much variation.
new_statements.domain_note: van Egmond: isolated (citation) word forms only; 'In connected discourse the stress patterns may be different due to higher-level targets.' Leeding: stress is a feature of the phonological word and shifts with suffixation and position in the phonological word; rhythm/timing outranks stress.
new_statements.identity_note: van Egmond 2012 describes Enindhilyakwa (= Anindilyakwa, anin1240) as spoken across Groote Eylandt (Angurugu/Umbakumba/Bickerton); Leeding's work is based mainly on the Umbakumba communalect, Stokes's on Angurugu. All are the same language-level languoid anin1240; no separate dialect glottocodes involved.

sources.locator: Chapter 2, section 2.4 'Stress', p. 27 (bullets pp. 27-28; summary p. 29)
sources.note: Penultimate syllable is the primary stress target (citing Stokes 1981, Leeding 1989), but stress is quantity-sensitive: /a/ and /ɛ/ (longer vowels) and closed syllables attract stress, so stress may (variably) retract to the antepenult when the penult has /i, ə/ and the antepenult has /a, ɛ/ or is closed; epenthetic vowels never stressed; pronominal prefixes on verbs get secondary stress; account 'preliminary', isolated word forms only; realisation = pitch + amplitude.

sources.citation: Leeding, Velma J. 1989. Anindilyakwa phonology and morphology. PhD thesis, University of Sydney. Section 2.13 Suprasegmentals, 2.13.2 Stress, pp. 139-142.http://hdl.handle.net/2123/1558
sources.note: p.139-140 (scanned of scan): 'Stress is a feature of the phonological word.. Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable in multi-syllabic words. More than one stressed syllable can occur in each word. Variant patterns for stress occur because maintaining the rhythm and timing is of greater importance than stress itself.. Stress falls on the first and penultimate syllables in most of the data. In words with an even number of syllables, the stress falls on alternate syllables, i.e., on the first syllable of each di-syllabic foot.' Trisyllables: penult, or initial if it has /a/ followed by…

sources.note: No dedicated stress section; in 1.2.3 Epenthetic vowels, p.157: 'in normal speech stress is always slight and never falls on the final syllable. In words of three syllables where both vowels in the first two syllables are either high or low, both vowels are evenly stressed. Otherwise only the low vowel is stressed. In words of four syllables the first and penultimate vowels are stressed.' Epenthetic vowel normally short and unstressed.
